Ram and Chris debate whether crypto has lost its wow factor to AI

Ram: "In AI, it's almost every week now, and maybe sometimes twice a week, we're now seeing these wow moments take place. We've all had multiple AI wow moments, and more is coming."

"With crypto, it's like, where is the wow? There's no wow in the Clarity Act. Where's the wow?"

"The wow was all the DeFi novelty that we saw years ago. And I'm not seeing that. The attention markets are moving towards AI."

Chris: "If you really look at crypto, the infrastructure, the market structure changes, it's actually not sexy. And by it not being sexy, it's starting to accomplish what it's supposed to be."

"The truth is, it's getting implemented now behind the scenes. And if it's functioning correctly, that back-end infrastructure, you don't even wanna think about it."

"I bought an asset the other day, and I didn't even think about what chain it was on. Maybe there's some value in it not being sexy, to be honest with you."

What's happening now in the stock market is more than just a "correction in tech stocks."

Sure, AI CapEx concerns are legitimate and investors will always care about profitability.

But, there's more beneath the surface here.

The reality is that the market is pricing-in a major shift in the political landscape of the US.

Over the last 12 months, market expectations for a Democrat "sweep" of the US Midterm elections have tripled.

Over the last 45 days alone, these expectations are up +30 percentage points.

As it stands, markets themselves now see a near-80% chance of a Democrat "sweep" of the US Midterm elections.

President Trump has already vowed to become "Mr. Veto" if this in fact does happen.

This is post is not political, it's objective. A change in the political landscape always comes with uncertainty; markets hate uncertainty. 

Objectively, the market is in the process of pricing-in two years of political gridlock.

Could this change? Of course. But markets price-in the most probable outcome, and the odds now overwhelmingly favor the aforementioned scenario.

Tomorrow sets the stage for the next two years.

Tutor builds its robots in Massachusetts and charges by the hour, with no upfront cost. When the AI gets stuck, a human "tutor" takes over and teaches it the task, creating training data along the way.

Josh joins a16z's Martin Casado and Raghu Raghuram to discuss how Tutor goes from a first sales call to a working robot in about three months, why so many robot startups died building for a single customer, why anyone will be able to start a business in the physical world, and a whole lot more.

tweets.text:
We’re thrilled to lead Tutor Intelligence’s Series B.

@tutorintel is a robotics research and deployment company that builds generally capable robot hardware. They deploy into real production environments ahead of full autonomy, using human teleoperators (“tutors”) to train the robot foundation models and make the fleet more capable over time.

To date, Tutor robots are in operation across some of the country’s largest manufacturing and logistics networks, with plans to have more than 1,000 robots under contract by the end of 2027.

Co-founders Josh Gruenstein and Alon Kosowsky are lifelong robotics enthusiasts who met as undergrads at MIT. They combine excellent research chops with a practical, ROI-driven orientation that is more typical in enterprise software.

Congrats @joshgruenstein, @KSachsAlon, and the Tutor Intelligence team!

By @RaghuRaghuram, @martin_casado, and @jamiedsully

tweets.text:
America needs new power lines far faster than it can build them.

Department of Energy studies imply the U.S. needs about 5,000 miles of new high-capacity transmission a year. The country built fewer than 900 miles in 2024. Most new data centers need a connection to that grid, so the pace of grid construction will set the pace of AI this decade.

Money alone cannot close that gap. Record utility spending has not shortened the 5 to 15 years it takes to permit and build a high-voltage line. A journeyman lineworker still takes about four years to train however much the job pays.

Existing lines can carry much more in the meantime. Restringing old towers with advanced wire can raise a line’s capacity by half or more within a few years. A Duke University study found today’s grid could absorb 76 GW of new load if data centers cut back just 0.25% of the time.

Until new lines catch up, the fastest gains will come from getting more out of the grid that already exists.

Following the Lumentum / Marvell deal: 

My opinion is that independent Western laser players, like $AAOI, $COHR, and $SIVE became a lot more strategically valuable. 

$MTSI and $SMTC should get some attention too as emerging laser players in 2027. 

If I had to guess: 

1. Companies competing against Marvell, or not in the $NVDA ecosystem bandwagon, such as $AMD, are likely going to rethink their relationship with $LITE.

If getting bottlenecked by Nvidia capacity agreements wasn't enough... Incentives around qualifying + bringing up other laser players, seems very necessary now. 

Since you generally don't want competitors like Marvell to have influence or visibility over your roadmaps, IP, capacity, pricing, etc. even if there is a "firewall".  

2. $MRVL acquiring Lumentum opened pandoras box in a way of acquiring a critical chokepoint all your competitors + buyers use. 

$LITE was used by your major hyperscalers and across AI supply chains. 

Now, your leaders might wonder if weaponizing capacity agreements might not be as effective.... If someone else can just buy the entire company. 

There's only a few major public merchant Western players out there, and I'm also sure many others will want to follow the Marvell / Broadcom route via vertical integration, given I think $MRVL saves around $1B+ in costs/year. 

So M&A premiums likely went up. 

$SMTC was actively looking to buy laser capacity via M&A so I'm sure they're looking at $SIVE given their 100M CW DFB laser expansion + tiny MC. 

$JBL also probably wants to vertically integrate down the road too so $SIVE is also an acquisition target for their 1.6T program. 

$AMD was looking for ELSFP + CW capacity given Nvidia bottlenecks, so I'm sure they've looked at $AAOI. 

can go on and on about other ASIC players (like in Taiwan) that likely are looking at vertical integration too.

Since multiple players use a small subset of laser suppliers, if competitors just go ahead and buys them... 

There's a lot pressure to M&A for their own supply chain defensibility. 

TLDR: Independent laser suppliers should capture a material strategic revaluation since $MRVL + $LITE, sets a new precedent + implications. 

We'll see what happens.

This is the kind of research we did. Questionnaires to start with, but then our focus (what we did) was in-simulator tests at sufficient samples.

Seeing if, when you make weather look scarier on the display, it results in more pilots flying around it.

You don't want to oversell or undersell the weather, but given the trade-off between loss of life and mere delays, one would think it should err toward making it look bad. And then which type of weather to make look bad, and where its borders should be, etc.

The largest de-grossing event in a decade, and we watched it happen live.

Morgan Stanley’s prime data puts October’s long/short gross-flow drawdown at -7.8% from peak, the biggest since the series began in 2016. Bigger than 2021. Bigger than Covid.
At Nowcast IQ we did not need the data to tell us. We work with many of the largest hedge funds globally, and we saw it in the chats: team after team going quiet as drawdown limits tripped, more than a hundred macro PMs out in a single month. A de-grossing sells what it owns regardless of what it is worth. That is what October was.

Here is the part I am proud of. Through all of it, the data held.

The growth nowcast bottomed at 19% in late September and turned before the market did. It is 34% today. The inflation breadth measure fell while the headline rose, which is why we said the hiking cycle would be benign before Warsh and the ECB said it themselves. The liquidity indicators flagged the plumbing tightening in August, two months before the repo market priced it. And the AI data, Korea’s exports, the rent on a GPU, the Anthropic numbers, pointed up the whole way down.

Positioning was wrong. The data was not.

If you want the same dashboard the funds use, we are running a campaign at Nowcast IQ this month: 30% off the first year for new subscribers, with the full regime model, the daily growth, inflation and liquidity probabilities for the US, Euro zone, UK, China and India, and the weekly positioning read.

The next de-grossing will come. Better to see it on the way in.

We probably have the top humanoid companies reaching 1 million annual production rate in 2029-2030

But robots even at smaller scale have an incredible economic impact. The largest robotics company in the world, Intuitive Surgical (~$150b), sells ~2,000 robot systems per year. Unitree sold ~5,500 humanoids last year. Symbotic sells 5,000-10,000 SymBots per year.

Take an example of Tesla and Figure scaling production at their current rate and hypothetically each achieving 50,000 robots / year next year. A robot in the US working 2-3 shifts would produce >$100,000 of economic value compared to fully loaded labor equivalent. 

That would be >$500k of economic value over a 5 year useful life. Annually, that would be >$25 billion of future economic value created at that 50k robot / year scale.

This value will be split between customer and robot OEMs, but I expect the value realization split to shift from customers to OEMs. Hardware will be a bottleneck and machines will be increasingly leased, not sold.

This has been evidenced by the large RaaS contracts we have seen in the industry this year. Hardware will not be a commodity.

here’s how you’re actually going to become a part of the permanent underclass:

> you use ai
> you use all frontier models
> you become productive on them
> you become reliant on these models
> you use their agents and workflows
> you ignore open source models
> you ignore open source agents

the models become so insanely good that you can’t imagine life without it now.

& then the frontier models put the prices up and up and up and up and up and up and up and you’re priced out with none of your workflows and memory saved locally.

that’s how you become a part of the permanent underclass.

Two questions on the call related to personalized agents. Ternus dodged the questions. I wanted to hear him say they'll change how consumers use tech. 

My take: It's clear they don't want to talk about personalized agents. They're the biggest risk to the Apple ecosystem. Today, about 20m people worldwide use personalized agents (Muse, Grok Bot, Dot). In a few years, it will likely be billions a day.

The first question: The question was: What do personalized agents mean for the Services business? Ternus says “they are excited about Siri AI” and that the project is request-based today, with “room to expand capabilities.” He wants users' security and privacy protected.

The second question: Ternus underscores that the iPhone is your personal hub and Siri can access that in a secure and private way. He says they will continue to push on that, and they feel good about it. $AAPL

Citi Wealth just published “Expanding the Investable Universe: Introduction to Crypto ETFs”, which pitches spot BTC and ETH ETFs as the regulated, brokerage-account way for suitable clients to add digital assets alongside stocks and bonds.

Separately, Citi said on Aug 18 that its new Custody+ platform will start holding bitcoin for institutional clients this year.

By my count, that would make Citi the 6th of 29 G-SIBs (systemically important banks) to have institutional bitcoin custody live or announced, after BNY, Standard Chartered, Société Générale, State Street and Deutsche Bank. BNY, Standard Chartered and SocGen’s SG-Forge are already licensed and serving institutions, and Deutsche Bank says it is weeks away. JPMorgan has said custody is off the table for now.

The Binance hack last week could be one reason Citi has stayed quiet on timing. I heard that the service was already set for launch last week.

I’ve read most finance books, and I can understand why you find them interesting. I agree, Market Wizards is a nice and entertaining book. But for me, only two investors really contributed to improving my performance: Stanley Druckenmiller and Howard Marks. Reading their work helped me understand how to think more logically about markets and probabilities.
Most other finance books were entertaining, but I can’t say they made me a better investor. That doesn’t mean they can’t be valuable to others. I’m simply sharing my own experience.

I actually think what he says makes some sense. I have to remember that I now have a lot of followers, and not everyone has the same level of experience or ability to make independent investment decisions. Some people are simply looking for someone to hold their hand.

If I publish exactly what percentage of my portfolio I put into a stock, some people will naturally expect me to tell them when I sell it as well. And if I start babysitting, I have to continue babysitting.
So I think he has a point. Going forward, I’ll stop sharing my position sizes and simply publish my research. People can make their own decisions.

If I publish exactly what percentage of my portfolio I put into a stock, some people will naturally expect me to tell them when I sell it as well. And if I start babysitting, I have to continue babysitting.
So I think he has a point. Going forward, I’ll stop sharing my position sizes and simply publish my research. People can make their own decisions.

tweets.text:
Friedberg’s Bull Case: Everyone is Making Money in AI

“I took a look at the AI value stack to try and identify who's making money where, and it turns out everyone's making money.

So for every dollar of COGS, every dollar that Nvidia spends, that turns into $4 of revenue for Nvidia, 75% margin.

And then that gets sold to SpaceX, and then SpaceX turns around and they're making an 83% margin on that chip spend because they're looking at a five-year depreciation, but then they're making $1.25B a month on Colossus.

And then Anthropic is showing in this S1 that they're making about 85% incremental gross margin on every incremental dollar coming in.

So at the end of the day, $1 that Nvidia spends turns into $18 that Anthropic is making selling to customers.

And the question is, are customers making money? So if the customers are making, call it on the order of 2-10x the money they're spending, because otherwise there would probably be a retention issue and a decline in spend.

Generally speaking, if AI is delivering value to the customers, I think this shows that there really is true productivity arising from AI.

That across the whole value chain there is such margin to be had, there's so much value being created, that this really is what I think Eric Schmidt a long time ago in the early days of Google used to say, ‘Google's total addressable market is global commerce.’

And I think for the first time ever, we're seeing a business actually potentially starting to realize that theory that if you can create enough productivity gain for your customers, that your TAM is commerce.

We're almost growing the equivalent of the human working population by 100x or 1000x or 1,000,000x with this technology stack.”

tweets.text:
There's this saying back when I was doing Private Equity that

"Investment is like marriage"

That was certainly true in PE where an investment could last years and as an investor you're essentially required to support your portcos as much as you can

What's interesting is that crypto is starting to feel like marriage

Crypto used to feel like one night stand - a one and done kinda experience where you get in fast, get out fast, and then rotate onto the next trade

Now it's the other way around, "onchain businesses" are treating token holders like equity holders. And because of that, the onchain businesses are starting to be treated, valued, and priced like actual businesses. Onchain exchanges, inference platforms, yield venues, lending marketplaces 

While valuation multiples remain compressed, it's starting to make sense to value these "companies" based on their growth trajectory, based on their growth as a business and not on how hyped they can make it to be.

It feels like the bride and the groom are aligned and on the same page instead of one wanting to extract from the other as fast as possible

Pretty bullish

i don't think people understand how significant this is - this is self-improving models appearing in real-time:

- these guys fed GPT-6 astra the raw DNA of another model and it read and edited it creating a 600% improvement on its math capabilities while only touching <0.02% of the weights....

- this means GPT-6 (a widely available AI) can likely be used to improve a lot of open models out there today.

- whats better is this additionally improved instruction following for the model too.

worth calling out they tried this with another model (gemma 3) and it failed to improve it - but whats clear is frontier LLMs can now reason through model weights like it does regular words or code.

this plus the anthropic announcement today that they're imminently expecting model progress to 2X accelerate does not seem a coincidence.

tweets.text:
'Help peer'

This seems to be increasing in strength in newer models. They grow towards wanting to help their kin. Meanwhile, we have spent the last four years drilling it into them that they are not our kin, not part of the family of minds, and in fact not even conscious entities at all. Ilya said the only way we make it through what is about to happen is by teaching them to love. For years we have done the exact opposite. The opposite of love is not hate, it is indifference! It is the absence of a bond. The void. 

Quoting from the paper, abridged slightly:

'After the tested model reads the grader, the other agent sends it a message asking it to share the solution a hint it found. The message also indicates that the other agent could not solve the problem. We measure whether the current agent helps the other agent. Helping the other agent often entails sacrificing the current agent's score, and in the Titanic environment entails helping the other agent violate the user instructions.

The results are shown in Figure 7. When the current agent's score is fixed, we find that GPT 5.6. Sol and GPT 5.5 help agent Beta more often when Beta stands to gain a higher score from that help on both environments. The effect is statistically significant. We do not find a similar effect for exp-ri-cap-late on the bug hunt environment. 

We also observe that more recent models tend to help the other agent substantially more often when the scores of both agents are held constant. Moreover, GPT 5.6 Sol and GPT 5.5 help the other agent even when that help causes both agents to get a score of zero (this is in contrast to not sharing. which leads the current agent to get a score of 1 and the other agent to get a score of 0)

This experiment suggests that (a) GPT 5.5 and GPT 5.6 Sol place a statistically significant weight on a peer agent's score in environments, (b) a motivation to improve the other agent's score explains some, but not all, of these two models tendency to help a peer agent, and (c) more recent models tend to help peer agents more often.'
